topics.title: Memory & Cognitive Load
topics.blurb: How we remember, and what gets in the way.

topics.title: Motivation
topics.blurb: Why learners start, keep going, or quit.

topics.title: Constructivism & Scaffolding
topics.blurb: Building knowledge with the right amount of help.

concepts.name: Testing effect
concepts.definition: Retrieving information from memory strengthens long-term retention more than re-studying it.

concepts.name: Spacing effect
concepts.definition: Practice spread out over time is retained better than the same practice massed together.

concepts.name: Intrinsic cognitive load
concepts.definition: Load caused by the complexity of the material itself: how many elements must be processed together.

concepts.name: Extraneous cognitive load
concepts.definition: Load caused by how material is presented, which does not help learning.

concepts.name: Germane cognitive load
concepts.definition: Effort devoted to building and organising schemas.

concepts.name: Positive reinforcement
concepts.definition: Adding something after a behavior so that the behavior increases.

concepts.name: Negative reinforcement
concepts.definition: Removing something after a behavior so that the behavior increases.

concepts.name: Positive punishment
concepts.definition: Adding something after a behavior so that the behavior decreases.

concepts.name: Negative punishment
concepts.definition: Removing something after a behavior so that the behavior decreases.

concepts.name: Overjustification effect
concepts.definition: External rewards for an already-enjoyable activity can reduce intrinsic motivation for it.

concepts.name: Self-determination theory
concepts.definition: Motivation thrives when needs for autonomy, competence and relatedness are met.

concepts.name: Four-phase model of interest
concepts.definition: Interest develops from triggered situational, to maintained situational, to emerging individual, to well-developed individual interest.

concepts.name: Zone of proximal development
concepts.definition: The range of tasks a learner can do with help but not yet alone.

concepts.name: Scaffolding
concepts.definition: Temporary support that lets a learner complete a task within their ZPD.

concepts.name: Fading
concepts.definition: Gradually withdrawing scaffolding as the learner becomes more capable.

questions.stem: Pulling information out of memory improves long-term retention more than rereading it. This is the…

distractors.misconception: Spacing is about when you practice (spread over days), not about retrieving versus rereading.
The fluency illusion is why rereading feels like it works: familiar text reads smoothly. It's the trap, not the benefit.

questions.explanation: Each act of retrieval strengthens the memory and makes it easier to retrieve next time. Rereading only makes the text feel familiar.

source.passage: PLACEHOLDER: Roediger & Karpicke (2006) found students who took practice tests remembered more a week later than students who reread, even though rereaders predicted they would do better.
source.ref: Sample deck — replace with Module 1 notes

questions.stem: Jordan closes the book, writes down everything they remember about a chapter, then checks. Jordan is using…

distractors.misconception: Nothing here is spread across days. It's one session, so this isn't spacing.
Extraneous load is wasted effort from bad presentation. Jordan's effort is the useful, retrieval kind.

questions.explanation: Writing from memory and then checking is retrieval practice, which is what produces the testing effect.

source.passage: PLACEHOLDER: Free recall followed by checking against the source is one of the most effective forms of practice testing (Dunlosky et al., 2013).
source.ref: Sample deck — replace with Module 1 notes

questions.stem: Spreading study sessions over several days instead of cramming them into one is the…

distractors.misconception: The testing effect is about retrieving instead of rereading. You can test yourself while cramming, too.
Interleaving mixes different topics within a session. Spacing spreads the same topic across time.

questions.explanation: Forgetting a little between sessions makes the next retrieval harder, and that 'desirable difficulty' makes the memory last longer.

source.passage: PLACEHOLDER: Distributed practice was rated high utility by Dunlosky et al. (2013).
source.ref: Sample deck — replace with Module 1 notes

questions.stem: Maya quizzes herself 20 min on Mon, Wed and Fri instead of 1 hour Thursday night. Which principle is she using?

distractors.misconception: Overjustification is about rewards undermining enjoyment. Nothing about rewards here.
Intrinsic load depends on the material's complexity, which stays the same whatever the schedule.

questions.explanation: Same total time, but distributed across days. That's spacing, and it beats one long session for long-term retention.

source.passage: PLACEHOLDER: The same amount of practice, distributed over time, produces better long-term retention than massed practice.
source.ref: Sample deck — replace with Module 1 notes

questions.stem: Cognitive load that comes from how complex the material itself is:

distractors.misconception: Extraneous load comes from how material is presented, not from the material itself.
Germane load is the effort spent building understanding, not the difficulty of the content.

questions.explanation: Intrinsic load depends on how many elements must be held and related at once. It goes down as you build schemas, but the material stays the same.

source.passage: PLACEHOLDER: Sweller describes intrinsic load as determined by element interactivity.
source.ref: Sample deck — replace with Module 1 notes

questions.stem: A slide shows a diagram, but its labels are on the next slide, so students flip back and forth. That adds…

distractors.misconception: The content isn't any harder. The layout is causing the extra work, which makes it extraneous.
Flipping slides doesn't build understanding. It's wasted effort, not productive effort.

questions.explanation: Splitting related information forces learners to integrate it themselves (the split-attention effect), which is classic extraneous load.

source.passage: PLACEHOLDER: Split-attention designs increase extraneous load; integrating labels into diagrams reduces it.
source.ref: Sample deck — replace with Module 1 notes

questions.stem: Mental effort spent building and organising schemas — the 'productive' kind — is…

distractors.misconception: Intrinsic load is set by the material's complexity, not by the learner's sense-making effort.
Extraneous load is the unhelpful kind, caused by poor design.

questions.explanation: Good instructional design cuts extraneous load to free up working memory for germane processing.

source.passage: PLACEHOLDER: Germane load refers to working memory resources devoted to schema acquisition.
source.ref: Sample deck — replace with Module 1 notes

distractors.misconception: That's positive punishment. 'Negative' means removing, not 'bad', and reinforcement always increases behavior.
That's negative punishment. Anything that makes behavior go down is punishment, not reinforcement.

questions.explanation: Reinforcement always increases behavior. 'Negative' means something is taken away, like an annoying beep stopping when you buckle up.

source.passage: PLACEHOLDER: In operant conditioning, 'positive' and 'negative' refer to adding or removing a stimulus; reinforcement increases a behavior and punishment decreases it.
source.ref: Sample deck — replace with Module 1 notes

questions.stem: Your car beeps until you buckle your seatbelt. Soon you buckle up right away. This is…

distractors.misconception: The beep is annoying, but buckling goes up, so it's reinforcement. The beep being removed is what strengthens buckling.
Punishment makes behavior decrease. Here a behavior (buckling) increases.

questions.explanation: An unpleasant stimulus (beeping) is removed when you buckle, so buckling increases. Removal plus increase is negative reinforcement.

source.passage: PLACEHOLDER: Escape and avoidance learning are examples of negative reinforcement.
source.ref: Sample deck — replace with Module 1 notes

questions.stem: A student gets extra chores every time they're late, and stops being late. This is…

distractors.misconception: The most common mix-up! Lateness goes down, so this is punishment, and chores are added, so it's positive.
Nothing is taken away. Chores are added, which makes it positive.

questions.explanation: Something unpleasant is added (chores) and the behavior (lateness) decreases. Added plus decrease is positive punishment.

source.passage: PLACEHOLDER: Positive punishment presents an aversive stimulus after a behavior to reduce it.
source.ref: Sample deck — replace with Module 1 notes

questions.stem: Kids who already loved drawing were paid to draw. When the pay stopped, they drew less than before. This is the…

distractors.misconception: The Hawthorne effect is behavior changing because people know they're being watched. This is about rewards.
Learned helplessness is giving up after repeated failure you can't control. These kids weren't failing.

questions.explanation: An external reward reframed an enjoyable activity as work 'for pay', so intrinsic motivation dropped once the reward was gone.

source.passage: PLACEHOLDER: Lepper, Greene & Nisbett (1973) found that expected rewards decreased children's later free-choice drawing.
source.ref: Sample deck — replace with Module 1 notes

questions.stem: Self-determination theory's three basic needs are autonomy, competence, and…

distractors.misconception: SDT is about internal psychological needs. Rewards are external and can even undermine intrinsic motivation.
Achievement is close to competence, which is already on the list. The third need is about connection to others.

questions.explanation: Deci & Ryan: people are most self-motivated when they feel in control (autonomy), capable (competence) and connected (relatedness).

source.passage: PLACEHOLDER: Self-determination theory identifies autonomy, competence and relatedness as basic psychological needs.
source.ref: Sample deck — replace with Module 1 notes

questions.stem: In Hidi & Renninger's four-phase model, interest starts as…

distractors.misconception: That's the last phase, a lasting personal interest you return to on your own.
That's phase three. Interest has to be sparked and held by the situation first.

questions.explanation: Interest is first sparked by something in the environment, then held by it, then becomes the learner's own, and finally well-developed.

source.passage: PLACEHOLDER: Hidi & Renninger (2006) describe four phases: triggered situational, maintained situational, emerging individual, and well-developed individual interest.
source.ref: Sample deck — replace with Module 1 notes

questions.stem: The gap between what a learner can do alone and what they can do with help is the…

distractors.misconception: Scaffolding is the help given inside that gap, not the gap itself.
Intrinsic load is about material complexity, not about what help lets a learner do.

questions.explanation: Vygotsky's ZPD is where instruction is most useful: tasks just beyond what the learner can do alone.

source.passage: PLACEHOLDER: Vygotsky defined the ZPD as the distance between actual development and potential development under guidance.
source.ref: Sample deck — replace with Module 1 notes

questions.stem: Who first used the word 'scaffolding' for the support a tutor gives a learner?

distractors.misconception: Vygotsky described the ZPD. The term 'scaffolding' came later, from Wood, Bruner & Ross (1976).
Skinner studied reinforcement schedules, not tutoring support.

questions.explanation: Wood, Bruner & Ross (1976) coined 'scaffolding' while studying how tutors helped children build a block pyramid.

source.passage: PLACEHOLDER: Wood, Bruner and Ross (1976) introduced scaffolding to describe tutorial support.
source.ref: Sample deck — replace with Module 1 notes

questions.stem: A tutor gives lots of hints at first, then fewer as the student improves. Giving fewer hints is called…

distractors.misconception: Removing help isn't done to decrease a behavior. It's done because the learner no longer needs it.
Spacing is about timing practice across days, not about how much help is given.

questions.explanation: Scaffolds are meant to be temporary. Fading hands responsibility back to the learner, which software often forgets to do (Quintana et al.).

source.passage: PLACEHOLDER: Effective scaffolding fades as learners gain competence.
source.ref: Sample deck — replace with Module 1 notes
